In [[mathematical analysis]], '''epi-convergence''' is a type of convergence for [[real-valued function|real-valued]] and [[extended real number line|extended real-valued]] functions. 

Epi-convergence is important because it is the appropriate notion of convergence with which to approximate minimization problems in the field of [[mathematical optimization]]. The symmetric notion of [[#Hypo-convergence|hypo-convergence]] is appropriate for maximization problems. [[Mosco convergence]] is a generalization of epi-convergence to infinite dimensional spaces.

== Definition ==

Let <math> X </math> be a [[metric space]], and <math> f_{n}: X \to \mathbb{R} </math> a real-valued function for each [[natural number]] <math> n </math>. We say that the sequence <math> (f_{n}) </math> '''epi-converges''' to a function <math> f: X \to \mathbb{R} </math> if for each <math> x \in X </math>

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_{n}(x_n) \geq f(x) \text{ for every } x_n \to x \text{ and } \\
& \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_n) \leq f(x) \text{ for some } x_n \to x.
\end{align}
</math>

=== Extended real-valued extension ===
The following extension allows epi-convergence to be applied to a sequence of functions with non-constant domain.

Denote by <math> \overline{\mathbb{R}}= \mathbb{R} \cup \{ \pm \infty \} </math> the [[extended real numbers]]. Let <math> f_n </math> be a function <math> f_n:X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}} </math> for each <math> n \in \mathbb{N} </math>. The sequence <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to <math> f: X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}} </math> if for each <math> x \in X </math>

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_{n}(x_n) \geq f(x) \text{ for every } x_n \to x \text{ and } \\
& \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_n) \leq f(x) \text{ for some } x_n \to x.
\end{align}
</math>

In fact, epi-convergence coincides with the [[Gamma convergence|<math>\Gamma</math>-convergence]] in first countable spaces.
=== Hypo-convergence ===

Epi-convergence is the appropriate topology with which to approximate minimization problems. For maximization problems one uses the symmetric notion of '''hypo-convergence'''. <math> (f_n) </math> hypo-converges to <math> f </math> if

: <math>\limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_n) \leq f(x) \text{ for every } x_n \to x </math>

and

: <math>\liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_n) \geq f(x) \text{ for some } x_n \to x. </math>

==Relationship to minimization problems==

Assume we have a difficult minimization problem 

: <math> \inf_{x \in C} g(x) </math> 

where <math> g: X \to \mathbb{R} </math> and <math> C \subseteq X </math>. We can attempt to approximate this problem by a sequence of easier problems

: <math> \inf_{x \in C_{n}} g_n(x) </math> 

for functions <math> g_n </math> and sets <math> C_n </math>.

Epi-convergence provides an answer to the question: In what sense should the approximations converge to the original problem in order to guarantee that approximate solutions converge to a solution of the original?

We can embed these optimization problems into the epi-convergence framework by defining extended real-valued functions

: <math>
\begin{align}
f(x) & = \begin{cases} g(x), & x \in C, \\ \infty, & x \not \in C, \end{cases} \\[4pt]
f_n(x) & = \begin{cases} g_n(x), & x \in C_n, \\ \infty, & x \not \in C_n. \end{cases}
\end{align}
</math>

So that the problems <math> \inf_{x \in X} f(x) </math> and <math> \inf_{x \in X} f_n(x) </math> are equivalent to the original and approximate problems, respectively.

If <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to <math> f </math>, then <math> \limsup_{n \to \infty} [\inf f_n] \leq \inf f </math>. Furthermore, if <math> x </math> is a limit point of minimizers of <math> f_n </math>, then <math> x </math> is a minimizer of <math> f </math>. In this sense,

: <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \operatorname{argmin} f_n \subseteq \operatorname{argmin} f. </math>

Epi-convergence is the weakest notion of convergence for which this result holds.

== Properties ==

* <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to <math> f </math> if and only if <math> (-f_n) </math> hypo-converges to <math> -f </math>.
* <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to <math> f </math> if and only if <math> (\operatorname{epi} f_n) </math> converges to <math> \operatorname{epi} f </math> as sets, in the [[Kuratowski convergence|Painlevé–Kuratowski sense]] of set convergence. Here, <math> \operatorname{epi} f </math> is the [[epigraph (mathematics)|epigraph]] of the function <math> f </math>.
* If <math> f_n </math>  epi-converges to <math> f </math>, then <math> f </math> is [[Semi-continuity|lower semi-continuous]].
* If <math> f_n </math> is [[convex function | convex]] for each <math> n \in \mathbb{N} </math> and <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to <math> f </math>, then <math> f </math> is convex.
* If <math> f^1_{n} \leq f_n \leq f^2_{n} </math> and both <math> (f^1_n) </math> and  <math> (f^2_n)</math> epi-converge to  <math> f </math>, then  <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges to  <math> f </math>.
* If  <math> (f_n) </math> [[uniform convergence | converges uniformly]] to  <math> f </math> on each [[Compact space|compact set]] of <math> \mathbb{R}_n </math> and <math> (f_n) </math> are continuous, then <math> (f_n) </math> epi-converges and hypo-converges to  <math> f </math>.
* In general, epi-convergence neither implies nor is implied by [[pointwise convergence]]. Additional assumptions can be placed on an pointwise convergent family of functions to guarantee epi-convergence.
